newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin-three weeks to recover from pneumonia.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin-three weeks to recover from pneumonia.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, a reluctant patient champing at the bit to return to work in the Kremlin, needs three weeks of rest to recover from a bout of pneumonia, according to his doctors.
The president's most popular rival, his former security chief Alexander Lebed, said on Friday that the illness had left the country adrift and issued fresh calls for Yeltsin to quit.

Politicians more sympathetic to Yeltsin, in hospital since Wednesday less than two months after heart bypass surgery, were generally silent. But some said his long absence from effective power proved the constitution had to be changed to shift power from the president to parliament.
Sergei Mironov, head of the Kremlin medical centre, said the president would spend three more days in Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital followed by three weeks of convalescence.

"Of course this is depressing him, of course his mood is not a very happy one, but I see no reason for particular pessimism," Mironov told a news conference. "He should have been brought here a few days earlier and we proposed this."
Mironov said the 65-year-old president had been weakened by the quintuple bypass surgery he underwent on November 5 but his immune system was functioning normally.
A Kremlin statement said Yeltsin's breathing had improved and his temperature and blood pressure remained normal but it was "too early to speak about a breakthrough".

Official announcements said the president, who had only just returned to work on December 23, sent congratulations to orphaned servicemen's children and honoured workers in the public prosecutor's office.

Lebed, sacked by Yeltsin for insubordination in October, said the president's new medical setback was "turning into a tragedy for the whole country. A power vacuum has been created...Now, as never before, it is necessary to rule the country, not to reign but to rule."
He said he aimed "to take power through civilised means" and predicted ultimate victory for his new political party.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who would take over for three months if Yeltsin stepped down, was on holiday near Moscow. Independent NTV television said the president's chief of staff Anatoly Chubais, reviled by Lebed as a 'regent' wielding vast power, had cancelled a trip to the United States.
Some mainstream politicians, uneasy over Yeltsin's long absence, sought change in the constitution, drafted after Yeltsin used tanks to quell a 1993 rebellion by parliament.

Yegor Stroyev, chairman of the Federation Council Upper House of parliament, made no reference to Yeltsin's illness but called for greater parliamentary control over appointments and economic policy. The country, he said, could no longer be run solely by decree.

"Many people understand that we cannot simply entrust power to a single person no matter how well we might think of him," liberal deputy Galina Starovoitova told NTV. "We need a redistribution of power between the various branches."

Russian financial markets ignored Yeltsin's illness. Leading shares soared to record levels on heavy volume as foreign investors poured money into Russia and some stocks rose by more than 10 percent during the day.
But a summit of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), grouping all former Soviet republics except the Baltic states, was postponed from January 19 until January 30-31.
Yeltsin had been due to attend the meeting but officials said the decision was not taken because of his health.
